preamble: Merger of the emphatic lateral with the emphatic sibilant: Proto-Semitic *ṣ́, reconstructed as an ejective lateral fricative [ɬʼ], fell together with *ṣ, reconstructed as the ejective affricate [tsʼ] (the view Kogan 2011: 62 calls most accepted; Wikipedia's consonant table gives [sʼ]), in Akkadian, Ugaritic and Canaanite, so that Hebrew ʾéreṣ 'earth' and ṣōʾn 'small cattle' have the same ṣādē as words with original *ṣ. Arabic (ḍād), Old South Arabian (a letter of its own) and the Modern South Arabian languages, where the sound is still a lateral ejective /ɬʼ/, keep it apart, and Aramaic turned it into ʿayin. Geʽez still writes ፀ (ṣ́) apart from ጸ (ṣ, /tsʼ/ in Wikipedia's Geʽez consonant table), but Gragg (1997: 244, quoted by Wikipedia) says the two have merged in the traditional pronunciation and in all modern Ethiopian Semitic, and that there is no evidence of the value ፀ had in Geʽez; Wikipedia's Ḍād article says the merger happened early. Tigrinya ዓጸደ 'reap', against Geʽez ዐፀደ, shows the merged spelling (Wiktionary). That Hebrew and Akkadian ṣ was still an affricate rests on transcriptions (Kogan 2011, cited by Wikipedia); later Hebrew traditions have [sˤ] or [ts]. The Proto-Semitic value is a reconstruction: whether the emphatics were ejective or pharyngealized is debated, since the daughter languages differ (pharyngealized in Arabic, Aramaic and Tiberian Hebrew, glottalized in Ethiopian Semitic and Modern South Arabian), though they are generally reconstructed as glottalized, i.e. ejective (Cantineau 1952; Kogan 2011: 61, as cited by Wikipedia; Wikipedia, Proto-Semitic language), and the most accepted view makes only *ṣ an affricate [tsʼ], leaving *ṣ́ a fricative [ɬʼ] (Kogan 2011: 62, cited by Wikipedia), while 'maximal' accounts reconstruct the affricate [tɬʼ]; the Greek rendering Mátlia of Geʽez ḍ has been taken as evidence for an affricate in Geʽez (Rodinson 1981 and Weninger 1998, per Kogan 2011: 80, cited by Wikipedia). This entry follows the [ɬʼ] of Wikipedia's Proto-Semitic consonant table.

examples.to: Hebrew אֶרֶץ ʾéreṣ, Phoenician 𐤀𐤓𐤑 ʾerṣ
examples.note: Arabic أَرْض ʔarḍ and Jibbali ʾɛrẓ̂ keep the lateral reflex distinct (Wiktionary).
